title: Critical Thinking · Episode 3
chapters: Small samples, big surprises: the law of small numbers
Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last
Berkson's paradox: when filtering creates false patterns

units.t: Critical Thinking. Episode three.

In this episode: Small samples, big surprises: the law of small numbers, How statistics can mislead, Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last and Berkson's paradox: when filtering creates false patterns.
Part one. Small samples, big surprises: the law of small numbers.
The places with the lowest cancer rates and the highest ones share the same surprising feature.
Understanding why will change how you read every ranking and review.
A puzzle about cancer maps.
Imagine a map of the United States showing kidney cancer rates by county.
The counties with the lowest rates are mostly rural and sparsely populated.
Fresh air, clean water, active lives?
Now look at the counties with the highest rates.
They are also mostly rural and sparsely populated.
Rural life can't be both protective and harmful.
The statistician Howard Wainer, and later Daniel Kahneman in Thinking, Fast and Slow, explained why: small counties have small populations, and small numbers bounce around far more.
Toss a fair coin four times and all heads happens about one time in sixteen.
Toss it 400 times and it is practically impossible.
Small samples crowd both the top and the bottom of any ranking.
The hospital question.
In the early 1970s Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman posed a question.
A town has two hospitals.
In the larger one about 45 babies are born each day, and in the smaller one about 15.
Roughly half of all babies are boys, but the exact share varies from day to day.
Over a year, each hospital records the days when more than 60 per cent of the babies born were boys.
Which hospital recorded more such days?
Most people said about the same.
The right answer is the smaller hospital, because with only 15 births a day, lopsided results are much more common.
In an earlier paper titled ‘Belief in the law of small numbers’, they had shown that even research psychologists trusted small samples too much.
The most dangerous equation.
The maths traces back to the 1700s and the French-born mathematician Abraham de Moivre.
In modern terms, the typical wobble in an average shrinks in proportion to the square root of the number of things being averaged.
That has a sobering consequence.
To halve the uncertainty in an estimate, you don't need twice as much data; you need four times as much.
To cut it to a tenth, you need a hundred times more.
Howard Wainer has called this ‘the most dangerous equation’, not because it's complicated, but because ignoring it has led to so many costly mistakes.
It explains why tiny trials, small surveys and short track records can be so misleading.
The small schools mistake.
Wainer's favourite cautionary tale involves American education.
From the late 1990s, reformers noticed that small schools were overrepresented among the top performers on test results.
Major funders, including the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, invested heavily in creating smaller schools and breaking up big ones.
But as Wainer and colleagues pointed out, small schools were also overrepresented among the worst performers.
Their results were simply more variable, because each year's scores came from fewer students.
Evaluations of the small-schools push produced mixed results, and the Gates Foundation later shifted its education strategy.
Whatever the other merits of smaller schools, the striking rankings had been at least partly an illusion created by sample size.
Reading rankings wisely.
Once you know this, you'll see it everywhere.
A new café with five reviews averaging five stars may be no better than an established one averaging 4.
6 from 2,000 reviews.
A footballer who scores in each of their first three games isn't necessarily a star.
A small study reporting a dramatic effect is more likely to be a fluke than a large study reporting a modest one.
A useful habit is to mentally pull extreme results from small samples back towards the average until more evidence comes in.
Statisticians have formal versions of this idea, sometimes called shrinkage.
And when you hear that a small town is the best or worst place for something, your first question should be: how many people live there?
The key idea: The places that look healthiest and unhealthiest are often the least populated, because small samples swing to extremes.
Part two. How statistics can mislead.
The numbers can be true and still tell a false story.
Here's how to spot the tricks.
Averages and extremes.
Most misleading statistics aren't lies; the numbers are accurate.
The deception is in what's included, what's left out, how it's compared and how it's shown.
The 1954 book How to Lie with Statistics by Darrell Huff became a bestseller because its tricks were so common.
Most still are.
The 'average' usually means the mean: add everything up and divide.
But extremes drag the mean around.
If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth of the customers soars, though nobody else got richer.
The median, the middle value when everything is lined up, is often more representative for skewed data like incomes and house prices.
When someone quotes an average, ask which one.
Percentages and pictures.
If an interest rate rises from 4 per cent to 5 per cent, that's one percentage point but a 25 per cent increase.
If support for something rises from 10 per cent to 15 per cent, that's 5 percentage points, or a 50 per cent increase.
Both are correct, and people choose whichever sounds more impressive.
A 200 per cent increase in something rare might mean going from 1 case to 3.
Graphs mislead too.
The classic trick is a truncated y-axis: starting at 95 instead of 0 makes a small change look like a leap.
A convenient start and end date can make a trend look up or down.
Two lines on different scales can seem connected.
Check the axis labels, starting point and timeframe before reacting.
Who is missing.
A statistic is only as good as its sample.
Online polls anyone can vote in attract people with strong opinions and can be flooded by campaigns.
In 1936, the Literary Digest polled millions, drawing largely on car owners and telephone directories, and those who replied leaned heavily one way.
It predicted a landslide defeat for Roosevelt.
He won by a landslide.
A well-designed random sample of around 1,000 is usually far more accurate than a huge biased one.
Survivorship bias is similar.
In World War II, the US military studied returning bombers to decide where to add armour.
Statistician Abraham Wald noted they only saw planes that survived: the areas without holes, like the engines, were where hits brought planes down.
Studying only successful businesses or old buildings still standing makes the same mistake.
Simpson's paradox.
Sometimes a trend that appears in every subgroup reverses when the data is combined.
In a well-known 1973 case, the University of California, Berkeley appeared to admit men at a higher rate than women overall.
But when researchers looked department by department, women were admitted at similar or higher rates in most departments.
The overall gap arose because women applied more often to highly competitive departments.
The lesson: how data is grouped can completely change its story.
Questions to ask.
When you meet a striking statistic, ask: Who collected it, and do they have an agenda?
How was the sample chosen, and how big was it?
Is it an average, and which kind?
Is it a relative or absolute change?
Compared with what, and over what time period?
What's left out?
Reputable sources, like the Australian Bureau of Statistics, publish their methods so you can check.
You don't need to be a mathematician to ask good questions about numbers.
The key idea: Accurate statistics can still mislead, and the median is often more representative than the mean when data is skewed.
Part three. Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last.
A footballer has a dream season, then a so-so one.
A new treatment seems to cure your worst week.
Often the real cause is a quiet statistical force.
The flight instructors.
The psychologist Daniel Kahneman told of teaching Israeli air force flight instructors.
One objected that praise works better than punishment.
When he praised an excellent manoeuvre, he said, the next attempt was usually worse.
When he shouted at a bad one, the next was usually better.
Kahneman realised the instructor saw something real but drew the wrong conclusion.
An unusually good flight is partly skill and partly luck, and luck tends not to repeat.
So the next attempt is likely to be closer to average, whatever the instructor says.
The same goes for unusually bad flights.
The praise and shouting were mostly irrelevant.
This pattern is called regression to the mean.
Skill plus luck.
Think of any performance as skill plus luck.
Skill is fairly stable.
Luck bounces around randomly.
When you pick out an extreme result, the very best or worst, you are partly selecting for skill and partly for unusually good or bad luck.
Next time the skill remains, but the luck is likely to be more ordinary, so the result moves back towards typical.
Crucially, no cause is needed.
Nobody got lazy or complacent.
The more luck matters, the stronger the pull to average.
Pure skill wouldn't regress; pure luck would regress completely.
Francis Galton noticed it in the 1880s: very tall parents tended to have tall children, but on average not quite as tall.
It describes groups, not destiny.
Curses and jinxes.
People joke about the Sports Illustrated cover jinx: athletes on the American magazine's cover often seem to slump soon after.
Similar talk follows big award winners and players who sign large contracts.
But think about when someone lands on a cover.
It is usually after a remarkable stretch, often their best ever, which almost certainly involved some good luck.
The following season is likely to be closer to their usual level, which looks like a slump by comparison.
No curse required.
The same logic applies to businesses praised after a record year, fund managers who topped the charts and restaurants that have just won an award.
Picking people at their peak practically guarantees an apparent decline afterwards.
Medicine and control groups.
When are you most likely to try a new remedy for back pain, a headache or a cold?
Usually when symptoms are at their worst.
Many conditions naturally fluctuate, so after a bad patch things are likely to improve somewhat, whatever you do.
If you took a remedy at the peak, it will seem to have worked.
That is a major reason researchers use control groups.
In a well designed trial, some patients get the treatment and others get a placebo or standard care, and both groups are chosen in the same way.
Regression affects both equally, so only a genuine difference between them shows a real effect.
This is general information, so speak to a health professional about your own situation.
Blackspots and big claims.
Imagine cameras installed at the intersections with the most crashes last year.
Next year, crashes there fall.
Success?
Partly, perhaps.
But some sites topped the list through an unusually unlucky year and would have improved anyway.
Road safety researchers account for this by comparing treated sites with similar untreated ones, or by using several years of data.
The trap also appears in schools, where extra help goes to the lowest scorers, and in workplaces, where struggling teams get a new manager.
So when something is chosen for being extreme, expect it to look less extreme next time, and ask what would have happened without the intervention.
Kahneman's instructors weren't wrong about what they saw, only about why.
The key idea: Praise seemed to make pilots worse and criticism seemed to make them better.
Part four. Berkson's paradox: when filtering creates false patterns.
Why do the best restaurants seem to be in the worst locations, and why do attractive dates seem more likely to be rude?
The answer is a sneaky trick of selection.
A strange hospital pattern.
In 1946, the American statistician Joseph Berkson pointed out a puzzle in medical research.
Among hospital patients, two unrelated conditions could appear linked, found together more or less often than in the general population.
The reason was how patients got into the data.
People are admitted because they have one condition or another, or both.
Studying only hospital patients filters the population by those very conditions, and that filtering alone can create a statistical relationship that doesn't exist in the wider world.
This is now called Berkson's paradox.
It is a cousin of selection bias, and once you know it, you spot it in dating, hiring, restaurants and headlines.
The dating puzzle.
The mathematician Jordan Ellenberg popularised this example.
Suppose someone will only date a person who is reasonably kind, reasonably attractive, or both.
In the general population, imagine kindness and looks are unrelated.
Now look only at the people this person actually dates.
Anyone neither kind nor attractive has been filtered out.
Among those left, the attractive ones only needed to clear one bar, so many aren't especially kind.
The kind ones are often not especially attractive.
Within this group, looks and kindness seem to be opposites, and it feels as though attractive people are more likely to be rude.
Nothing about the people changed.
The filter created the pattern.
Draw it to see it.
Picture a square scatter plot with talent along one axis and charm along the other.
If the traits are unrelated, the dots fill the square evenly, with no tilt.
Now add a rule: only people whose talent plus charm exceeds a certain total are admitted.
Draw a diagonal line across the lower left corner and remove every dot beneath it.
The remaining dots now slope downwards.
Among those who passed, the most talented tend to be less charming, and the most charming less talented.
A negative correlation has appeared from nowhere.
That is the essence of the paradox.
It also explains why great food can seem to hide in awkward locations: a restaurant in a bad spot survives only if the food is excellent.
Colliders and selection.
Researchers call a variable influenced by two other factors a 'collider'.
Filtering on it, or statistically controlling for it, can create a misleading link between those factors.
A well-known puzzle involves birth weight.
Babies of smokers tend to be lighter, and low birth weight raises risk.
Yet among only low birth weight babies, some studies found those born to smokers did slightly better.
Smoking wasn't protective.
Low birth weight can come from smoking or from other, often more serious problems, so comparing within that group mixed very different situations.
The same trap appears in admissions.
Among admitted students, a weak school record must be offset by a strong entrance test, so the test may seem to predict nothing.
Hiring shows it too, and in early COVID-19 studies of only tested or hospitalised patients.
Spotting the filter.
The key defence is a simple question: how did these cases end up in front of me?
If the group was selected on the very traits you're comparing, be suspicious of any pattern within it.
Your social circle, your newsfeed, a hospital ward, a list of successful companies and the people you have dated are all filtered samples.
Patterns within them may be produced by the filter rather than the world.
When possible, look at a broader, unfiltered group.
When that isn't possible, be careful about drawing big conclusions.
Data never simply speaks for itself.
It always arrives through some process, and understanding that process is half the work of understanding the data.
The key idea: Looking only at hospital patients can create links between diseases that don't exist outside.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do US counties with the lowest and the highest kidney cancer rates often share small populations?
Answer. Small populations swing to extremes by chance.
Question two. Why are median house prices usually reported instead of the mean?
Answer. A few extreme sales skew the mean.
Question three. Why did the flight instructor's criticism seem to work?
Answer. Poor flights were usually followed by average ones.
Question four. Why did hospital data suggest links between unrelated conditions?
Answer. Patients were admitted for those conditions.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
